metadata.title: Joe DiGenova Resigns From DOJ Investigation Into Alleged Conspiracy Against Trump

sources.news_title: The probe has drawn dozens of subpoenas but no charges, and diGenova left after clashes with senior Justice Department officials over its pace.

sources.text:
Mystery surrounds abrupt resignation of Trump loyalist leading DOJ’s conspiracy case against president’s enemies
Chief attorney tied to ‘grand conspiracy’ case suggests administration officials are trying to quickly prosecute the president’s foes
A longtime ally to Donald Trump who was tapped to lead a sprawling conspiracy investigation into the president’s political enemies abruptly resigned Thursday after the case failed to produce any indictments over the last year.
Joseph diGenova, the 81-year-old attorney who joined the president’s failed legal efforts to overturn 2020 election results, was hired by the Department of Justice in April to oversee an investigation into Trump’s chief grievances.
He submitted his resignation to Attorney General Todd Blanche this week amid alleged frustrations among prosecutors and the White House on the slow pace of the probe.
In an interview with The New York Post, diGenova said: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”
He later told the Associated Press that his quote was taken out of context, adding: “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”
diGenova has declined to comment further, adding only in a statement that it was an “honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department.”
He later told NBC News that “things were moving smartly” but “then things, you know, got where they got."
“The people in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Florida who are running this case have done a phenomenal job under the worst of circumstances,” he added. “I have no doubt that I was going to be able to take every one of these cases across the finish line because we we had put them in the perfect posture to proceed.”
Trump — after campaigning on a theme of “retribution” and pledging to be a “warrior” and “justice” to those who were “betrayed” by the government — has since publicly demanded criminal prosecutions of his political foes.
Last year, a top federal prosecutor in Florida reportedly issued more than two dozen subpoenas as part of a sprawling criminal inquiry into an alleged “conspiracy” among former officials who previously investigated the president.
Those subpoenas reportedly sought information and testimony from prominent officials close to intelligence reports alleging Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election, findings that the president has repeatedly labeled a “hoax” and a “witch hunt” against him.
The announcement of a grand jury — which was set to begin in January — signaled a wider investigation into what Trump’s allies have labeled a Democratic “conspiracy” against the president, including the federal law enforcement raid at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago compound and a federal indictment targeting his efforts to reverse his 2020 election loss.
But five months after diGenova took the reins of the investigation, it remains unclear what, if any, progress has been made.
“We are grateful to Joe diGenova for his many years of service to the Department,” a spokesperson for the agency told The Independent.
“The Attorney General thanks him for his work these past five months alongside the great team of experienced prosecutors in the Southern District of Florida, led by U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones,” the person said.
In November, Quiñones reportedly called a meeting of major crimes investigators after two top prosecutors resigned from his office over the handling of the investigation.
That same month, Trump ally Mike Davis — an influential legal ally to the president — said that his “buddy” Quiñones was preparing to impanel a grand jury that “should be fully up and running by January.” A court document noting the grand jury appeared to confirm the investigation.
Career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long was reportedly forced off the case after she allegedly resisted pressure to quickly bring charges against former CIA director John Brennan.
DiGenova, who represented Trump during his 2020 campaign and throughout the Russia investigation, was brought on in April as “counselor to the attorney general.”
Also assigned to the case is Christopher-James DeLorenz, a former clerk to District Judge Aileen Cannon during the Mar-a-Lago investigation who was transferred to south Florida from Washington, D.C.
Cannon — a Trump appointee — dismissed the Mar-a-Lago case against the president, who was accused of illegally withholding classified documents at his home and then obstructing law enforcement efforts to get them back.
She is the only judge in Ft. Pierce district in Florida, where a bulk of the “grand conspiracy” case appears to be playing out.
FBI Director Kash Patel, meanwhile, has assembled an alleged “payback squad” composed of agents willing to target Trump’s supposed foes and handle politically charged cases.
A senior FBI official has denied that such a group exists with that name but confirmed the existence of the Director’s Advisory Team, which was launched last year to dive into internal documents and other government materials in an effort to expose and discredit federal law enforcement officials who investigated Trump and his allies.
That team was uncovered by members of Congress last year. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, discovered that the group had a written list of names targeting FBI officials and agents who were “in the crosshairs” for forced retirement or removal from the bureau. The group now appears to be linked to the investigation in Florida.

Hackiest prosecutor Trump could find not hacky enough
Joseph diGenova was brought in to prosecute Donald Trump’s deep state enemies, after the DOJ prosecutor who was originally given this Stalinesque task was fired, for reporting to her superiors that she couldn’t find any evidence of a deep state conspiracy against Donald Trump. Todd Blanche figured that diGenova would be up for the job, given his impeccable complete MAGA hack credentials, but sometimes a man, even an 81-year-old man, ends up caring more about holding onto his law license, and not ending up like Rudy Giuliani:
Counselor to the Attorney General Joe diGenova abruptly resigned Thursday from a sprawling probe into former officials in the Obama administration, The Post has learned.
“I did resign today by letter to the attorney general. I said that it was a privilege and an honor to serve the president and the department, and I was very grateful,” diGenova told The Post by phone on Thursday night.
DiGenova was investigating Obama-era figures who allegedly pushed claims of collusion between Donald Trump and Russia during the 2016 presidential campaign,
Sources said diGenova had lost support from Department of Justice leaders and the White House amid his “grand conspiracy” investigation, with one source suggesting that the 81-year-old prosecutor and former Trump defense lawyer was “slow-rolling” indictments and getting lost down “rabbit holes.”
Asked whether he had lost focus, diGenova dismissed the accusation and shot back: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”
Having “ethics,” even of the most self-interested kind, is definitely suboptimal in the Trump DOJ. Too bad Natalie doesn’t have a law license (yet).

Joe diGenova has abruptly resigned from the Justice Department role he took just five months ago, leaving a major Florida-based investigation without the veteran prosecutor who had been overseeing it.
The 81-year-old former U.S. attorney confirmed Thursday that he submitted his resignation directly to Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“I did in fact resign,” diGenova told the Associated Press, describing it as an “honor and a privilege” to serve President Trump and the Justice Department after a five-month return to government that included responsibility for the Florida-based inquiry.
DiGenova initially declined to explain the circumstances. In a later interview, however, he pushed back on criticism that the investigation was moving too slowly amid reported frustration inside the Justice Department and White House over the pace and management of the probe.
“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” he said.
DiGenova then clarified that he believes there is evidence supporting the prosecution theories under review, but said the cases require more time to develop.
“There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution,” he told the AP. “It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”
The AP reported that diGenova’s exit came five months after he returned to the department. A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to the outlet’s request for comment.
The resignation also followed new subpoenas seeking testimony before a federal grand jury in Florida, signaling that at least parts of the investigation were still active.
The AP noted that diGenova had served as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia during the Reagan administration and had publicly argued for years that intelligence officials conspired against Trump. He had asked then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to appoint him to the investigation.
Investigative journalist John Solomon, who spoke publicly about the departure, said disagreements over resources, strategy and access to evidence are common inside the department.
Joe diGenova resigned today as lead prosecutor in the Fort Pierce case. But not for the reasons some in the legacy media are saying. Yes, disagreements over resources, strategy and access to evidence are common inside DOJ.
— John Solomon (@jsolomonReports) September 11, 2026
The resignation came as grand jury activity appeared to be accelerating.
CBS News reported that attorneys for several witnesses had recently been notified that their clients would receive grand jury subpoenas. Investigators also sought voluntary interviews with lawyers representing former FBI agents involved in the classified-records investigation of President Trump.
The inquiry, based in Fort Pierce, Florida, has examined whether officials from the Obama and Biden years participated in a broader effort to use federal law enforcement and intelligence powers against Trump.
One strand centers on former CIA Director John Brennan and the intelligence community’s 2017 assessment of Russian interference in the 2016 election. The larger inquiry has also examined other investigations involving Trump, including the FBI’s 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago.
No criminal charges have resulted from diGenova’s investigation.
Joe diGenova abruptly resigns from DOJ after overseeing "grand conspiracy" probe into Biden and Obama officials. https://t.co/k49iVdFPRp
— CBS News (@CBSNews) September 10, 2026
DiGenova’s return to government was publicly announced in April.
The Justice Department announced on April 20 that he had been sworn in as counselor to the attorney general, a senior advisory role covering major legal, policy and enforcement matters.
At the time, U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones praised diGenova’s experience and judgment.
DiGenova previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia from 1983 to 1988 under President Ronald Reagan. He later built a high-profile private legal practice.
The department’s announcement credited him with supervising public-corruption, national-security and violent-crime prosecutions during his earlier government service. It said his new advisory duties would draw on that experience as well as his work in complex investigations and private practice.
No charges had been filed when diGenova resigned.
BREAKING: Prosecutor Joe diGenova, who led the “grand conspiracy” probe of Trump targets, resigns without charging anyone. https://t.co/3wrZ1072HU
— NBC News (@NBCNews) September 10, 2026
CBS reported that diGenova’s wife, attorney Victoria Toensing, who also worked with the Fort Pierce team, plans to leave the Justice Department on Friday.
The Justice Department had not publicly named a replacement as of Friday afternoon.
That leaves two immediate questions hanging over the investigation: who will take charge, and whether the department’s timetable will change after diGenova’s warning that prosecutors cannot rush the evidence needed to bring a case.

Trump ally quits his DOJ ‘grand conspiracy’ probe
DiGenova had been hired in April, soon after Pam Bondi was fired as attorney general
What happened
Joseph diGenova, a former federal prosecutor and ally of President Donald Trump, resigned Thursday from the Justice Department, where he was leading a wide-ranging conspiracy investigation into Trump’s perceived political foes. DiGenova was hired in April, weeks after Trump fired Attorney General Pam Bondi amid his “repeated expressed frustration” with her “pace — and limited success — in overseeing efforts to target his rivals,” The Washington Post said. He’s departing “amid mounting frustration from the Justice Department and White House over the pace and management of the probe,” The Associated Press said.
Who said what
The Florida-based investigation, which Trump’s allies call the “grand conspiracy,” is the “most fevered of the many revenge investigations” Trump has “demanded” from the Justice Department, The New York Times said. It “hinges on an unusual and untested legal theory,” the Post said: “that previous administrations conspired for years to violate Trump’s rights through a series of investigations.”
“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” deGenova told the New York Post Thursday. He later told the AP there was “plenty of evidence,” but “it just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others.”

A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.
Say It Ain’t So, Joe!
Joseph diGenova, the Trump loyalist and conspiracy promulgator put in charge of the sweeping DOJ investigation into an imagined grand conspiracy against the president, abruptly resigned yesterday reportedly under pressure for not having secured indictments quickly enough.
For a brief moment last night, diGenova looked like he might effectively turn whistleblower against the Trump DOJ. “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” he told the New York Post.
But a short time later, diGenova backtracked somewhat, telling the AP that his comments were taken out of context: “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”
Victoria Toensing, diGenova’s wife who was also part of the prosecution team, is resigning, too.
What to make of all this?
We don’t have perfect visibility into how it all came down, but the Trump track record on retributive prosecutions is pretty clear and diGenova’s departure fits into the general pattern:
- Trump just wants indictments. More than anything else, President Trump is eager to stain his foes with indictments. What about actual convictions? That would be icing, but they are almost beside the point. This approach of indict first and try to build a case later is so at odds with how legit prosecutors operate that it remains a cognitive obstacle to analyzing what is going on in the Trump retributive prosecution cases. (You’d also expect a genuine tyrant to want his foes jailed, not merely indicted, so having convictions be an afterthought is confounding on many levels.)
- Trump Sends Underlings Into the Buzzsaw. Indicting first and then trying to build a case later puts the onus on Trump DOJ prosecutors on the front end and exposes them to the full wrath of the judiciary on the back end. It is a no-win situation for them. We’ve seen this again and again, with judges excoriating prosecutors for not being ready with discovery, slow-rolling cases after indictment, and generally still working to compile their case as it barrels towards trial.
- Churning Through Underlings. To get around putting prosecutors in impossible positions with judges, the Trump DOJ frequently churns through junior prosecutors in the same case. It makes it hard for judges to hold prosecutors to account when they’re no longer on the case. Senior Trump DOJ officials have in some cases had to step into the breach themselves. It’s further reduced the capacity of the Justice Department, often leaving political appointees on the front lines in big cases, a nearly unheard of rarity at DOJ.
- Todd Blanche Knows the Score. Blanche became attorney general because President Trump wasn’t satisfied that Pam Bondi was moving fast enough against his foes. Blanche used his time as acting attorney general to ramp up the second prosecution of James Comey over the seashells arrayed to say “86 47” and to take other aggressive steps on Trump’s behalf — including appointing diGenova to jumpstart the grand conspiracy investigation — and thus lock down the nomination to the permanent position.
- Blanche Brought in diGenova. Bondi was gone by early April, and by late April Blanche has installed diGenova in a much-touted move to bolster the languishing (and bogus) grand conspiracy investigation, which is being run out of the Miami U.S. Attorney’s Office.
- diGenova Wasn’t the First Prosecutor to Quit this Case. Before diGenova arrived on scene, career DOJ prosecutor Maria Medetis Long had withdrawn from the case, reportedly over concerns that the evidence was insufficient to charge former CIA Director John Brennan in a companion case.
- diGenova is No Saint in all of This. A staple of GOP politics since he served as D.C. U.S. attorney in the 1980s, diGenova had taken an opportunistic turn toward the Trumpian right over the past decade. He was an attractive option to lead the grand conspiracy investigation because he’d been touting various MAGA conspiracy theories publicly as a Trump surrogate on TV and privately as a legal adviser to the president on matters related to the Russia probes.
- diGenova Saw the Writing on the Wall. His resignation came after clashes with higher-ups at Main Justice, including reportedly being told that “he had lost the confidence of his superiors,” CNN reported.
- diGenova Gives Defense Attorneys a Gift. diGenova’s comments to the NY Post will be damaging in any subsequent prosecution that arises from the grand conspiracy investigation. It is more evidence of vindictive prosecutions by the Trump DOJ, and could be used as an example in other unrelated prosecutions as an example of the pattern of DOJ misconduct.
- diGenova Beats Hasty Retreat. DiGenova’s walkback to the AP of his earlier remarks is still somewhat damaging to DOJ, but it also shows diGenova hastily returning to the fold, where it’s easier to stoke conspiracy theories, gin up Trump, and overpromise results than it is to actually build a viable criminal case that can win a conviction and withstand appeal. That requires real evidence, professional prosecutors, hard work, and adherence to the standards of legal ethics.
Trump wants what he wants: the stain of indictment on his foes, the same as he was stained. He doesn’t care if he breaks the Justice Department, ruins prosecutors careers, churns through appointees, or fails to obtain a conviction. That’s it. It’s not that complicated.

DHS Deletes Super Racist Post
The Department of Homeland Security has taken down a post that featured Optimus Prime of Transformers fame wearing the DHS seal on his armor and telling a Sikh man to “Self Deport or Find Out.” DHS said the post was referring to Harjinder Singh, an Indian trucker who has been demagogued by the Trump administration for his involvement in a fatal highway crash last year in Florida. Hasbro, which owns the Transformers brand, was not happy about the DHS post either.
The Post-9/11 Tools Now Used At Home
On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, The Washington Post’s Warren Strobel picks up a theme that has been a key part of TPM’s coverage of Trump II: “[P]owerful agencies and vast legal authorities created to stop another terrorist catastrophe are being turned inward, with the Trump administration using many of those powers to round up immigrants, battle drug traffickers and target political dissent.”

Detectorist Finds Hoard of Viking Coins
I am a sucker for these kinds of stories every single time.
An amateur with a metal detector last week found the largest hoard of Viking Age coins ever unearthed in Finland.
The stash of silver coins has not been cleaned or counted yet, but it weighs about 10 pounds. That’s more than twice the weight of Finland’s previous largest Viking Age coin hoard, which was found in 1895 and contained some 1,700 coins.
The newly discovered hoard was really three discoveries in one. Kalle Lappinen, the detectorist, first found one cache, then another about 40 feet away. Each cache was buried about a foot and half below the surface inside of its own birch-bark container, an interesting find in its own right.
The NYT has reaction from professional archaeologists.
